historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Insulins and insulin analogues

starting.description: Pancreatectomy-induced diabetes localized a crucial antidiabetic function to the pancreas and motivated a search for its internal secretion. Banting describes Baron's observation of duct obstruction as the immediate stimulus for a ligation-and-extraction plan, which the team tested in diabetic dogs.

inspiration.description: Experimental pancreatic diabetes, observed responses to pancreatic duct obstruction, and a hypothesized endogenous pancreatic secretion led investigators to make extracts from animal pancreas.

steps.description: Experiments and observations linked pancreatic loss to diabetes, initiating a search for an internal secretion and its antidiabetic effects.
Toronto researchers obtained active pancreatic extracts in diabetic dogs; Collip worked on purification for human administration, with clinical responses reported in 1922.
Biosynthetic human insulin and amino-acid engineering created rapid-acting and longer-acting analogues of the known active hormone, with distinct approaches to controlling absorption and duration.

design.description: Investigators devised extraction and purification, then recombinant manufacture and insulin-sequence or acylation modifications. Rapid-acting analogues reduce self-association; long-acting analogues use slower depot release or multihexamer formation and albumin binding. These target pharmacokinetics while retaining an established insulin template and activity.

circumstances.description: The Toronto ligation and extraction experiments were deliberately planned to obtain the putative antidiabetic secretion, regardless of whether the initial ligation hypothesis was correct.

limits: Lispro and aspart are rapid-acting insulin analogues; glargine and degludec are longer-acting analogues with different protraction mechanisms. The class record does not adjudicate every analogue's development priority.
Banting's extraction plan was one contribution to a multi-investigator history of pancreatic diabetes and extracts, not the first observation that an animal pancreatic extract could lower glucose.
conflicts: The S1 figure caption says the first January 11 injection had no effect; S2 reports biochemical changes but no clinical benefit. S2 is more specific about the contemporaneously measured observations.

Banting's retrospective S3 treats the first duct-ligated extract as supporting the enzyme-destruction idea; S1 describes subsequent evidence that duct ligation was not necessary. The idea is recorded as motivation, not as a validated requirement.

S4's introduction gives 1992 for the January 23 human treatment where S2 dates the event to 1922. S4 also describes glargine's added B-chain arginines as amino-terminal; S5 and the USP glargine monograph identify the carboxyl terminus instead. The record does not adopt either erroneous detail.
gaps: Original reports of earlier pancreatic extraction and the individual analogue programs were not all reopened; causal synthesis uses the explicitly labeled retrospective sources and the 1922 clinical original.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: Reported pancreatic changes with gallstone duct obstruction helped suggest Banting's duct-ligation and extraction strategy.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: Clinical pathology qualifies here as observation of naturally occurring disease; subsequent dog experiments and biochemical purification were essential.
